script:
Part One

My name is Hamad. Last term, our class began a heritage walking tour after noticing a problem that affected people around us. We wanted to do something useful rather than simply prepare an attractive display. Our teacher asked us to explain our purpose, identify the people who might benefit and plan what resources we needed. We held our first meeting at the old souq. Students had different ideas about the best approach, but we agreed that accurate information would matter more than finishing quickly.

We divided the tasks between several small teams. Some pupils prepared questions and checked documents; others organised materials and contacted people who could give reliable advice. We used a printed map, but soon discovered that equipment alone could not guarantee a successful result. A local guide helped us examine the evidence, ask better questions and plan realistic steps. We recorded decisions in a shared notebook so that nobody would forget what had been agreed.

Part Two

Our first attempt revealed a street name printed incorrectly. At first, one student suggested leaving the mistake because correcting it would take extra time. I disagreed, and we returned to a road sign and an official map to find out what was actually correct. We changed the relevant information and explained the reason for our decision. That experience taught us checking historical sources and respecting privacy. We also understood why a group should welcome careful criticism instead of treating every question as a personal attack.

After preparing the visitor route, we invited visiting families to examine it. Some people were pleased, while others suggested clearer wording and additional practical details. We listened to their comments and made adjustments where the evidence supported them. We did not expect every visitor to have identical needs, so we tried to explain our work in accessible language. The team held another meeting to discuss what had gone well and what should change.

By the end of the term, I understood that a successful school project involves more than a final product. It requires cooperation, responsible decisions and willingness to correct mistakes. Our class hopes the activity will support more responsible tourism. I have become more confident asking questions when an explanation is unclear. I also know that sharing work publicly creates a responsibility to respect other people and present reliable information.
